title: Inquiry Opens Into the Death of Mohamed Anas Bennis
subtitle: Mohamed Anas Bennis died on December 1, 2005, in the Côte-des-Neiges neighbourhood of Montreal. He was shot twice by the Montreal Police Service (SPVM).
article: A public inquiry opened Wednesday at the Laval courthouse into the death of Mohamed Anas Bennis, who died on December 1, 2005, in Montreal's Côte-des-Neiges neighbourhood after being shot twice by the Montreal Police Service (SPVM).
At the time, two SPVM officers, Jonathan Roy and Yannick Bernier, were walking to the site of an operation when they crossed paths with Mr. Bennis.

In testimony given Wednesday afternoon, Officer Bernier said he didn't have time to react when the man, who was only a metre away, pulled out a knife and held it to his throat. A struggle followed, and the two men ended up on the ground.

Officer Bernier said he fired two shots after ordering the man to "drop" his knife. "I remember taking the time to analyze the situation and realizing there was nothing else I could do to protect myself," he testified.

Officer Abderazak Bouhenniba, who was waiting for the two patrol officers a few metres away, testified that he heard the suspect shout "God is great" in Arabic, raising his fist in the air before striking Officer Bernier. "I knew something was happening and I immediately called for backup before rushing to help Yannick," said Mr. Bouhenniba.

Three eyewitnesses to the scene testified Wednesday, including Daniel Doiron, who was on his way to work at the time. He said he saw Mr. Bennis pin the officer to the ground and hit him in the face "like a madman" with a knife. According to this witness, Mr. Bennis did not comply with orders to stop, and the officer then opened fire.
The two other witnesses, both women, did not notice that the suspect had a knife. Officer Bouhenniba also said he did not see the knife until he was right next to them.

In her opening remarks, Coroner Catherine Rudel-Tessier said she would not allow "anyone to look for scapegoats," and that the purpose of the inquiry was to clarify unanswered questions and determine whether the man's death could have been avoided.

These comments appeared to upset the Coalition Justice for Anas. The Coalition was denied the right to participate in the inquiry as an interested party, but will be able to address the coroner during the final submissions.
"We have more than a hundred questions we would have liked to ask the officers involved and the investigators," said spokesperson François Du Canal.
"Quebec's justice system is being held hostage by the police organization," said the victim's father, Mohamed Bennis. "It is impossible for a citizen to win when police officers are involved."
The Coalition also represents the victim's father, who chose to wait outside the courtroom even though he had come specifically from Morocco.
The Quebec City Police Service, which conducted the investigation at the time, concluded that no blame could be assigned to the officers.
